title: 29  Comparison and Extended Binary Numbers
text:
In this section, we show we can compare an input integer ciphertext \(c\) with \(0\), meaning a function which outputs \(1\) if \(c > 0\) and \(0\) otherwise. (it will be clear how to do variants of this, such as with nonstrict inequalities). Our main trick is to use what we call the extended binary expansion of \(c\).
Define \(S_1 := {-1,0,1}.\) We say that a number \(a\) is in extended binary form if it is represented as \[
a = a_0 + a_1 2 + \cdots + a_{b-1}2^{b-1},
\]
where each digit satisfies \(a_i \in S_1.\)






TipRemark (\(S_1\)): 



The main intuition is this: we need the slightly larger digit set \(S_1\) because the difference of two ordinary binary numbers has digits in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). This avoids needing to perform carrying, which is hard in CKKS.


Now:

Assume that we have the extended binary digits of \(c\) as \(c_0, c_1, \ldots, c_{b-1},\) in little-endian order, where each \(c_i \in S_1\).
We construct the functions “\(\geq 0\)” and “\(=0\)” on the finite set \(S_1\). Since \(S_1\) is finite, these functions are polynomials on \(S_1\)! (furthermore, with operations that are not likely to accumulate a lot of floating point error)

For example, on \(S_1\), the function \(\mathbf{1}_{x > 0}\) is given by \[ \frac{x^2+x}{2}. \] Indeed, this is \(0, 0, 1\) at \(x=-1, 0, 1\) respectively.
Similarly, the function \(\mathbf{1}_{x=0}\) is given by \(1 - x^2.\)

This allows us to construct a comparison function on the space of extended binary numbers. The key logic is that an extended binary number \[ a = a_0 + a_1 2 + \cdots + a_{b-1}2^{b-1} \] is positive if and only if at least one of the following events occurs: \[
a_i = 1 \quad\text{and}\quad a_{i'} = 0 \text{ for all } i' > i. \] In words: the most significant nonzero digit of (a) is positive.

Therefore,
\[
\mathbf{1}_{a>0} = \bigvee_{i=0}^{b-1}
\left(
(\mathbf{1}({a_i=1})
\wedge
\bigwedge_{i' > i} \mathbf{1}({a_{i'}=0})
\right).
\]
To see the formula decide a comparison, take \(x = 1011_2 = 11\) and \(y = 0110_2 = 6\). The orange digit is the most significant nonzero digit of the difference, which is the one that decides the sign.

\[
\newcommand{\ebeTop}[1]{\textcolor[RGB]{230,159,0}{\mathbf{#1}}}
\]

\[
\begin{array}{l|cccc|c}
& i=3 & i=2 & i=1 & i=0 & \text{value}\\
\hline
x & 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 & 11\\
y & 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 6\\
x-y & \ebeTop{1} & -1 & 0 & 1 & 5\\
\mathbf{1}(d_i=1)\prod_{i'>i}\mathbf{1}(d_{i'}=0) & \ebeTop{1} & 0 & 0 & 0 & \mathbf{1}_{x>y}=1\\
\hline
y-x & -1 & 1 & 0 & -1 & -5\\
\mathbf{1}(d_i=1)\prod_{i'>i}\mathbf{1}(d_{i'}=0) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \mathbf{1}_{y>x}=0
\end{array}
\]
Step 1. The digits of \(x-y\) are \(d_i = x_i - y_i\), so \((d_3,d_2,d_1,d_0)=(1,-1,0,1)\), and indeed \(8-4+0+1=5\).
Step 2. The term for \(i=3\) is \(1\cdot 1 = 1\), because no higher digit exists, so the OR is \(1\) no matter what the lower digits do. The lower terms are \(0\) because each has a nonzero digit above it, so \(x>y\).
Step 3. Swapping gives digits \((-1,1,0,-1)\). The digit \(d_2=1\) is blocked by \(d_3=-1\neq 0\), so every term is \(0\) and \(y>x\) is false.
The logical AND and OR operations can themselves be written as polynomials on Boolean values:
\[
A \wedge B = AB,
\]
and
\[
A \vee B = 1 - (1-A)(1-B).
\]
Thus the comparison function can be implemented as a polynomial in the extended binary digits.
Since the intermediate values are essentially Boolean or integer-valued, this construction avoids the main numerical instability of trying to compare arbitrary real CKKS values directly.

title: 30  Index To One-Hot
text:
Using roots-of-unity, we can do a one-hot conversion function (this will be used later for sorting). Specifically, given a ciphertext input for integer \(i\), stored in root-of-unity form (from this point we use \(\sqrt{-1}\) to distinguish from \(i\)) \[
\zeta^i = e^{2\pi i \sqrt{-1}/k},
\] where \(\zeta = e^{2\pi \sqrt{-1}/k},\) we wish to create a one-hot vector \(v\) which is \(1\) in the \(i\)-th coordinate and \(0\) elsewhere. We can do this as follows:

Create a vector \(v'\) whose \(j\)-th coordinate is \(\zeta^{-j}\).
Multiply entrywise by \(\zeta^i\): \(v'' = v' \cdot \zeta^i.\)
Then the \(j\)-th coordinate of \(v''\) is \(\zeta^{i-j}\). In particular, the \(i\)-th coordinate is (1), while every other coordinate is a nontrivial \(k\)-th root of unity.
For each entry \(w\) of \(v''\), compute \[1 + w + w^2 + \cdots + w^{k-1}.\] This expression equals \(k\) if \(w = 1\) and equals \(0\) if \(w\) is a nontrivial \(k\)-th root of unity.
Therefore, after dividing by \(k\), we obtain the desired vector \(v\).

title: 31  Discrete sign and notes on sorting
text:
31.0.1 Sign function
Suppose we know that our data consists of integers in the range \([-b,b]\), and we want to create a sign function. Notice that modulo \(2b+1\), a number in the range \([-b,-1]\) is equivalent to a number in the range \([b+1,2b]\). Likewise, a positive number sits in the range \([1,b]\).
So, if our inputs are stored as residues modulo \(2b+1\), we can create a sign function by interpolating a polynomial which sends \(1,\ldots,b\) to \(1\), \(b+1,\ldots,2b\) to \(-1\), and \(0\) to \(0\).
Alternatively, if our values are stored as roots of unity, let \(\xi\) be a primitive \((2b+1)\)-st root of unity. Then interpolate on the discrete points \(\xi^0,\ldots,\xi^{2b}\), sending \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^b\) to \(1\), \(\xi^{b+1},\ldots,\xi^{2b}\) to \(-1\), and \(\xi^0=1\) to \(0\). This gives us the sign of the original integer directly from its root of unity representation.


31.0.2 Comparisons
We can use this lookup idea to compare entries without binary expansion. Suppose our integers lie in \([-b,b]\). Their differences lie in \([-2b,2b]\), so for comparisons we use the larger modulus \(n=4b+1\) and let \(\xi\) be a primitive \(n\)-th root of unity.
Construct a polynomial \(S\) by interpolation such that \[
S(\xi^d)=
\begin{cases}
0, & d=0,\\
1, & 1\le d\le 2b,\\
-1, & 2b+1\le d\le 4b.
\end{cases}
\]
Figure 31.1 shows \(S\) for \(b=3\), so \(n=4b+1=13\). Each point on the circle is \(\xi^d\), which stands for a difference \(d\) between two entries, and the label on the point tells you which \(d\). The value \(S\) gives is the sign of \(d\): the orange arc (\(d=1,\ldots,6\)) is the positive differences and gets \(+1\), the blue arc (\(d=7,\ldots,12\)) is the negative differences and gets \(-1\), and \(d=0\) gets \(0\). The blue arc holds the negatives because \(\xi^{d}=\xi^{d-13}\), so \(d=7,\ldots,12\) is the same as \(d=-6,\ldots,-1\).








Figure 31.1: The sign polynomial \(S\) on the \(13\)th roots of unity (\(b = 3\)). Each point \(\xi^d\) encodes a difference \(d\), and \(S\) returns its sign. The grey point \(\xi^0\) (difference \(0\)) gives \(0\), the orange arc \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^6\) (positive differences) gives \(+1\), and the blue arc \(\xi^7,\ldots,\xi^{12}\) (negative differences \(-6,\ldots,-1\)) gives \(-1\).





Given an \(m\)-length vector \(W\), where \(W_i=\xi^{a_i}\), we can compare entries \(W_i\) and \(W_j\) by computing \[
s=S\left(W_iW_j^{n-1}\right).
\] Since \[
W_iW_j^{n-1}=\xi^{a_i-a_j},
\] we get \(s=1\) if \(a_i>a_j\), \(s=-1\) if \(a_i<a_j\), and \(s=0\) if they are equal.
If we only want to know whether \(a_i>a_j\), we can compute \[
c=\frac{s^2+s}{2}.
\] However, we can also interpolate this comparison directly. Construct a polynomial \(C\) such that \[
C(\xi^d)=
\begin{cases}
1, & 1\le d\le 2b,\\
0, & d=0 \text{ or } 2b+1\le d\le 4b.
\end{cases}
\] Then \[
c=C\left(W_iW_j^{n-1}\right)
\] gives the same comparison result without the extra squaring step. This still uses only \(n\) interpolation points, since the input is the encoded difference.


31.0.3 Bubble sort
We can use bubble sort as a starting point. Bubble sort passes through a given vector, performing repeated pairwise comparisons and swaps.
To sort from smallest to largest, compare neighboring entries \(W_i\) and \(W_{i+1}\) using \[
c=C\left(W_iW_{i+1}^{n-1}\right).
\] Then \(c=1\) if the entries are out of order and \(c=0\) otherwise.
To swap the entries without branching, define \[
W_i'=(1-c)W_i+cW_{i+1},
\] \[
W_{i+1}'=cW_i+(1-c)W_{i+1},
\] leaving every other coordinate unchanged. Both expressions use the original entries. Thus, when \(c=0\), nothing changes; when \(c=1\), the entries swap.
Perform this operation on pairs \((1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)\). These \(m-1\) comparisons move the largest integer to the final position, still encoded as a root of unity.
Repeat on the first \(m-1\) entries, then the first \(m-2\) entries, and so on. After \(m(m-1)/2\) comparisons, the vector is sorted by the \(a_i\)s.
The same PairSort operation can also be used in odd-even and bitonic sorting networks.


31.0.4 Sorting by rank
Alternatively, we can use the comparisons to find each entry’s final position directly. For distinct inputs, an entry’s rank is the number of inputs smaller than it: \[
r_i=\sum_{j=1}^m q_{ij},
\qquad
q_{ij}=C\left(W_iW_j^{n-1}\right).
\] These comparisons are independent, so they can be computed in parallel.
We can reduce the number of comparisons by comparing only when \(i<j\). The diagonal entries are always \(0\), and, assuming distinct inputs, each entry below the diagonal is \(1\) minus its reflected entry: \[
q_{ji}=1-q_{ij}.
\] Then we count across rows as before. This gives \(m(m-1)/2\) comparisons instead of \(m^2\).


31.0.5 Alternative idea for one-hot vectors
Instead of encoding the ranks as roots of unity, we could keep them as encrypted integers.
For each possible rank \(j\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\), let \(L_j\) be the interpolated polynomial sending \(j\) to \(1\) and every other rank to \(0\). Then \[
[L_0(r_i),L_1(r_i),\ldots,L_{m-1}(r_i)]
\] is the encrypted one-hot vector for entry \(i\).
To get the sorted vector, multiply each one-hot vector by its corresponding encoded entry and add: \[
\sum_{i=1}^m W_i
[L_0(r_i),L_1(r_i),\ldots,L_{m-1}(r_i)].
\] The output remains encoded as roots of unity.
If we only want the minimum, maximum, or median, we do not need the full one-hot vectors. We can evaluate only the polynomial for the position we need. For example, \[
\sum_{i=1}^m W_iL_0(r_i)
\] gives the encoded minimum, while \[
\sum_{i=1}^m W_iL_{m-1}(r_i)
\] gives the encoded maximum. For an odd number of entries, the median is at rank \((m-1)/2\).

TipSummary




A discrete representation of numbers is useful to have as a substitute / in addition to the standard input. Can consider writing down the “digits” as integers or as the roots of unity.

With each choice, certain things become much easier (or at least doable) such as the sign / inequality function, but certain things become harder as well (such as addition or multiplication).

text: Here, we collect some miscellaneous functions and extensions of previous sections we found interest in during our explorations.

title: 33  Dot Products and Matrix Multiplication
text:
Let us work with square matrices for simplicity. A client gives us \(A, B \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\) and we want to compute \(C = A \cdot B\). For simplicity, we assume that the rows of \(A\) and the columns of \(B\) are given. If we only have rows of \(B\), we can tweak them to obtain columns.
Recall the dot product of two vectors \(x = (x_1, \dots , x_n)\) and \(y = (y_1, \dots , y_n)\) is defined as \(x \cdot y = x_1y_1 + \dots + x_ny_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i\).

Suppose we had two encoded vectors \(x\) and \(y\). We can obtain the vector \(x*y = (x_1y_1, x_2y_2, \dots, x_ny_n)\) with element-wise multiplication.
We then perform an intravector sum to obtain a vector \[v(x,y) = \mathtt{sum}(x * y) = (d,d,\ldots, d),\] where \(d = x \cdot y\).
We can then e.g. multiply it with a \(1\)-hot mask vector \((0, 0, \ldots, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)\) or use it in any other way we wish.

This directly lets us compute the entries of the \(n \times n\) matrix \(C = A \times B\), since those are dot products:

let the encoded first row of \(A\) be denoted \(A_1 = (a_{11}, a_{12}, \dots, a_{1n})\) and the encoded first column of \(B\) as \(B_1 = (b_{11}, b_{21}, \dots, b_{n1})\).
As just stated, we can get \(c_{11}\), the \((1,1)\) entry of \(C\), by just taking the dot product \(A_1 \cdot B_1\). In general, we can get \(c_{ij} = a_i \cdot b_j\), though underneath the hood we are actually getting vectors of the form \(v(A_1, B_j) = (c_{ij}, c_{ij}, \ldots, c_{ij})\).

To get actual row / column vectors of \(C\), we could get the entries, take some dot products by \(1\)-hot vectors, and add. Specifically, if we wanted the \(i\)-th row vector \(C_i\), we would add \[ (1, 0, \ldots, 0) * v(A_i, B_1) + (0, 1, \ldots, 0) * v(A_i, B_2) + \cdots + (0, \ldots, 0, 1) * v(A_i, B_n). \]
It is possible that we may want to use a different representation of the matrices. For example, let \(A\) be arranged such that each row \(a_i\) is stored contiguously in ciphertext \(A'\): \[A'=(a_1,a_2,...a_n)=(a_{11},a_{12},...,a_{1n},a_{21},a_{22},...,a_{nn})\]
Likewise \(B\) with columns \(b_j\), denoted \[B' = (b_{11},b_{21},...,b_{n1},b_{12},b_{22},...,b_{nn})\]
Using these initial \(n^2\) ciphertexts as an example: \[A'*B' = (a_{11}b_{11},a_{12}b_{21},
         ...,a_{1n}b_{n1},a_{21}b_{12},
         ...,a_{n,n-1}b_{n-1,n},a_{nn}b_{nn}).\]
Now, we claim that if we can extend summing to do a \(k\)-th “partial” intravector sum for a \(mk\)-vector \(x\): \[\begin{align}\mathtt{partsum}(x,k) = & (x_1 + \cdots + x_k, \cdots, x_1 + \cdots + x_k, \\
& x_{k+1} + \cdots + x_{2k}, \cdots, x_{k+1} + \cdots + x_{2k}, \\
& \vdots \\
& x_{(m-1)k+1} + \cdots + x_{mk}, \cdots, x_{(m-1)k+1} + \cdots + x_{mk})
\end{align}\]
we would be able to use \(\mathtt{partsum}(n, A'*B')\) to compute \(n\) of the correct terms; for example, \((A \times B)_{1,1}\) in position \(1\). If we repeat this \(n\) times after cycling \(A'*B'\) (by \(n\) each time), we can combine them to get the final vector. As a concrete example for \(n=2\):

title: 34  Shannon Entropy
text:
Suppose we have a discrete random variable \(X\) with possible outcomes \(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\) each with corresponding probabilities \(P(x_1), P(x_2),\dots,P(x_n)\).
The Shannon entropy1 is defined as
\[H(x):=-\sum_{i=1}^nP(x_i)\log P(x_i),\]
where \(P(x_i)\) represents the probability of each outcome \(x_i\).
First, commenting on the input: 1. Shannon entropy only works on a probability distribution, so all the input must be non-negative and add up to 1. 2. For sake of focus, we will assume that this is already solved. 3. Otherwise, this seems to be a routine case of a “normalization step” where each user input is divided by their sum, which is a combination of a sum and a division of the form \[
P(x_i)=\frac{x_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j}.
\]
We should then end up with a vector \(x = (P(x_1), \ldots, P(x_n))\).
Now, we need the logarithms of the probabilities. These can also be done in various ways; when applicable, we black-box the details, deferring to previous sections: 1. we can use a Taylor series approximation, centered necessarily away from \(0\). 2. we can have the user simply give the \(\log(x_i)\) as part of their input.
In any case, we should end up with a vector \(l\) with each \(l_i = \log(P(x_i))\).
Then it suffices to compute the element-wise product \(x * l * (-1)\) to obtain a single vector, after which using a sum operation gives \[H(x):=-\sum_{i=1}^nP(x_i)\log P(x_i)\] (or more precisely, a vector where every element is \(H(x)\)).
The main difficulties while computing entropy arise in situations where \(x_i = 0\). In this case, L’Hopitals rule dictates that the correct contribution of the \(-P(x) \log P(x) = 0 * (\infty)\) should be \(0\). We have two suggestions, and it is not clear to us which one is better (it is likely to be very implementation-dependent): 1. “iron out” the eventual answer with multiplication by an \(\texttt{equal(x\_i, 0)}\) vector at the very end (before the summation), which would ensure all elements coming from an \(x_i\) very close to \(0\) actually contributes \(0\); 2. interrupt the computation right before the \(\log()\) step by adding the \(\texttt{equal(x\_i, 0)}\) vector, which would switch the \(x_i\)s close to \(0\) to close to \(1\) (therefore making the \(\log(x_i) \approx 0\).
In production, any method would require extensive testing to prevent blowup.

title: 35  “Adaptive” Division
text:
We cannot do If statements, but we can encode If statements with sign functions. Here’s a design that might work and require some testing, but gives an idea of how we might do “adaptive” computations unadaptively:

For simplicity, we assume the number to invert, \(x\), is positive and within the region \([1, 2^{16}]\).
We try to make a function that is essentially “the largest power of \(2\) smaller than \(x\)”

Suppose we have an idealized sign function, then consider the following sum, where \((x > k) = \mathtt{sign}{(x-k)}\) is a sign indicator function (so it is \(1\) if the comparision is TRUE, and \(0\) otherwise): \[ - \frac{1}{2^{15}} (x > 2^{15}) - \frac{1}{2^{14}}(x > 2^{14}) + \cdots - \frac{1}{2}(x > 2) + 1.\]
Note:

if \(2 > x \geq 1\), it returns \(1\) since none of the comparisons are true.
if \(4 > x \geq 2\), then it returns \(1-1/2 = 1/2\).
if \(8 > x \geq 4\), then it returns \(1 -1/2 - 1/4 = 1/4\).
…the idea is that it will return \(1/2^n\) if it is between \(2^{n+1}\) and \(2^n\).

This essentially creates a “guess” in \(\log(b)\) steps (for transparency: each step is a sign call and so may be expensive), where \(b\) is an upper bound of \(x\). The method needs tweaking for numbers under \(1\) or negative numbers, which we omit.

title: 36  Logarithm (Revisited)
text:
In Section I we showed how to get logarithms via Taylor expansion. In addition to that standard approach, we explored a distinct iterative method that seems interesting, though not immediately practical, using some niceness particular to the log function.
Suppose we have \[ n \leq \log_2(x) < n+1, \] using the inverse relationship between the logarithm and exponentiation, this can be rewritten as: \[ 2^n \leq x < 2^{n+1}.\] If we define \(m = \frac{x}{2^n}\) (so \(x = m \cdot 2^n\)), we can divide both sides by \(2^n\) to obtain \(1 \leq m < 2\). Using \(m\), we can write \[ \log_2(x) = \log_2(m \cdot 2^n). \] This effectively breaks up the log into two components: a real and a fractional part, which can be treated separately. In other words, this is noticing that if \(x = m \cdot 2^n\), where \(m \in [1,2)\), then \[\log_2(x) = \log_2(m \cdot 2^n) = n + \log_2(m).\]
As a first iteration of this strategy, we can approximate only in the range \([1,2)\) and add back a scaling factor later. As an example, to compute \(log_2(20)\), we can compute \(log_2(1.25)+4\) instead. The \(n\) part can be given or “solved for” in a method similar to the previous section VII.3 to “detect” the largest \(n\) such that \(2^n < x\).
With the strategy just mentioned, we break the log function into an integer and fractional part. Afterwards, we can deal with the fractional part with a “fixed point iteration” method using binary representations.
Suppose \(y = \log_2(m)\), and written as \(y = 0.b_1b_2b_3\cdots,\) (in other words, \(y = b_1/2 + b_2/4+b_3/8 \cdots\)). Note that if we square \(m\), \(y\) shifts by exactly one decimal point to \[2y = b_1.b_2b_3b_4\cdots.\]
As a result, we are able to find the binary represenation, one bit at a time. For example, if \(u = m^2\), then \(u \in [1^2, 2^2) = [1,4)\). This allows for \(\log_2(u) \in [0,2)\) This process helps us create our iteration: \[
|b_k| = \begin{cases}
    0, & \text{if } u_k < 2 \rightarrow \log_2(u_{k-1}) < 1 \\
    1, & \text{if } u_k \ge 2 \rightarrow \log_2(u_{k-1}) \ge 1
\end{cases},
\] after which we can recover \[
\sum_{i=-m}^{k} b_i \, 2^i, \quad \text{where } b_i \in \{0,1\}.
\]






TipConcrete Example



We work through some explicit initial iterations as an illustrative practice. Take \(x=0.75\). We aim to obtain an approximation of \(\log_2(0.75)\). Rewriting \(x\) in the desired form \(x = m * 2^n\), we see that \(n = -1\) and \(m = 1.5\).
In the first iteration, squaring \(m\) gives \(2.25>2\) hence the first bit is \(1\), and we must renormalize, dividing \(2.25\) by \(2\) resulting in \(1.125=u_1\). For the second iteration, squaring \(1.125\) we get \(1.265625<2\) so our next bit is \(0\) and we do not need to renormalize.
If we continue iterating twice more we would obtain the binary digits \(1001\), which we interpret as the fractional part of a binary number, corresponding to the value \(0.5625\). This is our approximation for \(\log_2(m)\). We now add \(n= -1\) to give an initial approximation for \(x\) as \(-0.4375\). For reference, the actual value is approximately \(-0.4150\). We can get closer to the actual value of \(x\) with a higher number of iterations, but recall that with more iterations, we naturally have performed more computations, so error accumulates.
